entries.title: Backfire diagnostic: did the correction actually strengthen the false belief?
entries.summary: Backfire is a narrow outcome, not a synonym for disagreement, defensiveness, or misinformation that remains partly influential after correction. This guide turns the concept into a testable decision pattern.

diagnostic.label: 1. Define the target belief
diagnostic.text: Write the exact factual claim and, when possible, record confidence before the correction. If the target changes during the conversation, you cannot tell whether the original belief backfired.

diagnostic.label: 2. Correct the same claim
diagnostic.text: Use a clear correction from a source the audience has a reason to treat as credible. A correction that is not understood or trusted can fail, but failure alone is not backfire.

diagnostic.label: 3. Measure direction, not emotion
diagnostic.text: Ask whether belief in the corrected false claim became stronger. Anger, argument, source distrust, or refusal to concede are different outcomes unless the factual belief itself increased.

diagnostic.label: 4. Check again later
diagnostic.text: Immediate correction effects can weaken with time. A delayed check helps separate a short-lived response from durable belief updating or continued influence.

distinctions.text: Corrected misinformation can still shape later reasoning even when belief in it has fallen. That persistence is not automatically a backfire effect.
People may resist when a message feels controlling or autonomy-threatening. Reactance can affect persuasion, but it does not by itself show that the corrected factual belief became stronger.
Goals and prior attitudes can steer how evidence is evaluated. This is a broader processing pattern; backfire is one possible belief-change outcome, not another name for motivated reasoning.
Repetition can increase perceived truth through familiarity. It is a different phenomenon from a correction increasing belief in the false claim.

playbook.label: Correct rather than surrender
playbook.text: The evidence does not support a rule that corrections usually make misinformation stronger. Avoiding corrections because of a generic fear of backfire throws away a tool that usually improves factual accuracy.

playbook.label: Make the correction easy to identify
playbook.text: State what is wrong and what the more accurate account is. When misinformation supplied a causal explanation, a coherent alternative can help fill the explanatory gap left by the retraction.

playbook.label: Treat format as secondary
playbook.text: Fact-first and myth-first formats have not shown a large, universal performance gap once the essential correction is present. Spend more effort on clarity, evidence, and whether the correction is actually received.

playbook.label: Separate belief from downstream attitudes
playbook.text: A correction can improve factual accuracy without changing identity, policy preference, trust, or behaviour. Measure the outcome you care about instead of treating all resistance as one construct.

playbook.label: Use delayed verification
playbook.text: For consequential claims, re-check the factual belief later. Misinformation can continue to influence reasoning after a correction even when an immediate belief measure improves.

systemChecklist: Immediate confidence in the same claim
Delayed confidence in the same claim
Separate measures for source trust, attitude, or behaviour
Outcome label: corrected, unchanged, backfire, or continued influence
